claims.kickoff_quote: Then dispatch the accessibility-tester agent; it only reads.
claims.skill_quote: Do not fix code unless the dispatcher asks — report and recommend.
claims.reasoning: This clause echoes the skill's own no-fix rule, but its function in context is operational, not pedagogical: it is placed right after the design-reviewer paragraph which explicitly flags that design-reviewer 'writes that baseline file, so it is not read-only and does not share a browser with the others' — i.e. it tells the orchestrator this agent has no such exclusivity/commit constraints and can be sequenced freely. That is ordering/parallelism information the rubric explicitly carves out as load-bearing, not duplication, even though the underlying fact also happens to appear in the skill's Output section.

claims.kickoff_quote: Then dispatch the accessibility-tester agent; it only reads. Give it its conformance target explicitly — WCAG 2.1 AA unless this project committed to something stricter — so it is not inferring the bar it is grading against.
claims.skill_quote: Establish the application structure, target audience, and compliance target (default WCAG 2.1 AA).
claims.reasoning: The skill already defaults to WCAG 2.1 AA when no target is given, so the bare value overlaps with the skill's own default. But the operative clause — 'unless this project committed to something stricter' — is project-specific knowledge (whether this particular project's requirements exceed the default) that the skill has no way to know on its own; this is exactly the conditional-gating-the-operator-must-judge case the rubric calls out as load-bearing, not duplication.

claims.kickoff_quote: This is a gate: tell me plainly whether it passed, because a failing scorecard blocks the ship.
claims.skill_quote: State the conformance level achieved and any residual limitations.
claims.reasoning: The skill's own output contract is a severity-sorted findings report plus a stated conformance level — a narrative, not a binary verdict. Casting that as a pass/fail gate that blocks the ship is a milestone-workflow decision the reusable skill deliberately has no opinion on (it doesn't know it's being used as a ship gate at all), so this is orchestration-level framing load-bearing to KICKOFF's process, not a restatement of the skill's own methodology. Searched the file for gate/pass/fail/scorecard/block terminology (grep for 'pass', 'fail', 'gate', 'scorecard', 'block') and found none, confirming the gate framing originates entirely from KICKOFF.
